paras: The lynching of an unnamed Black man in Webster Parish, Louisiana, was a killing reported in the national press in August 1880, in which a number of citizens took a prisoner accused of murdering his wife from the officers holding him and shot him to death. The only account, a brief miscellany item, said the man was struck by more than twenty bullets and that none of the parties' names were known.

According to the brief, a Black man in Webster parish was accused of murdering his wife and was arrested for the crime the following day. The item named no town, gave no date for the killing, and did not identify the man, his wife, the officers or the citizens involved.

While in custody, the man was said to have tried to escape and to have "severely wounded two of his guards." At that point "a number of citizens" took him from the officers and killed him by firing more than twenty bullets into his body. The brief did not say how many people took part, whether the officers resisted, or where the shooting took place.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage, and the brief itself stated that "the names of none of the parties are known."

The Daily Globe printed the item on August 22, 1880, in its "Facts and Fancies" column, between a joke about a saloon-keeper and an anecdote about an exploding kerosene lamp. It carried no headline or dateline, stated the accusation against the man as fact, and offered no comment on the killing. The Bismarck Tribune in Dakota Territory ran the same item on August 27 in its "Items of Interest" column, again alongside the kerosene-lamp story.
No Louisiana newspaper account and no coverage in the Black press were found.

accounts.label: Unsourced miscellany brief
accounts.gist: A Black man arrested for killing his wife wounded two guards trying to escape, and a number of citizens took him from the officers and shot him more than twenty times.

framing.detail: The Daily Globe ran the item in its 'Facts and Fancies' column among jokes and curiosities, stating the accusation as fact and offering no comment on the killing.
The Bismarck Tribune carried the same item in its 'Items of Interest' column.

record_check.dossier: The brief reports two deaths if the wife is counted (the wife and the accused man); only the accused was killed in the mob violence, and the two guards were wounded, not killed.
The brief describes a group taking a prisoner from officers and killing him, which meets the definition, though from a single unsourced report.
Not stated; known only to precede printing on 1880-08-22, so it may have occurred earlier than August.
One unnamed Black man; the brief says no names are known.
